ARAHA · 0:28–0:50 Why? Loneliness, and a lack of community. Seventy percent of students in halls feel lonely or isolated, and the heaviest social media users are the loneliest. Yet young people say they want to support the local places around them. Every week there's a formal, a match, a night out, and most of us only hear about it the morning after. Say the last sentence to the room, not the slide. The numbers are there for the audience to read. If asked: the 100% figure is from a survey by Faire, a marketplace for independent shops, reported by MarketingCharts: every Gen Z respondent said they would take some action to help local businesses, and about 7 in 10 would shop locally more often. The 70% figure is from a poll by Opinium for PfP Students, a student accommodation company; a third of students said they feel that way often. The 38% figure is from a study of 65,000 US college students in the Journal of American College Health (Taylor and Francis): those on social media 30 or more hours a week were 38% more likely to report loneliness than those who did not use it.

JACOPO · 1:30–2:30 (five scenes, one per press; the first starts by itself) 1 · This is BNOC. You join in seconds with your university email, and choose your communities: your college, your society, your sports team, or the E-Lab cohort. Each has its own questions, table and prizes. (press) 2 · The questions come from the members. Anyone can propose one; organisers approve it before it goes live. (press) 3 · Then you make your call, and say how confident you are. The app weighs everyone's confidence and shows you, live, what the crowd thinks as it shifts. (press) 4 · When the answer comes in, being right earns points, and points move you up the table. Know your community best, and you're the Big Name On Campus. (press) 5 · And the table leads somewhere real: prizes you redeem in person at local businesses. A game on your phone that ends with you walking through a real door. How it works: each press plays one scene, then the picture waits for you. Pressing while a scene is still moving jumps to the end of that scene. The left arrow goes back a scene, R replays the current one, and the five dots at the bottom show where you are. After scene 5, the next press moves on to Alexander's slides. Honest note: choosing between several communities and redeeming in the app are the next things we are building; today the pilot runs one community. If asked, say so.

ALEXANDER · 3:08–3:40 So who pays? Never the players. Local venues pay a hundred pounds to run a challenge with their own prize. Employers and brands sponsor calls to fill their events. Students' unions pay for their own leagues. And at scale, ads in the rewards section. One campus is worth about thirty thousand pounds a year. Our ask is ten thousand pounds, to reach every college and our first ten paying venues. WHY EACH ONE PAYS 1. Local venues (cafés, pubs, clubs). £100 buys one challenge: a call about their own place, with their own prize, in front of every player in the community. It is one simple price a café owner can say yes to on the spot, and the redemption code in the demo shows them who actually walked in. At a café making about £3 on each sale, it pays for itself if about 35 extra customers come in. The first challenge is free during the pilot, so they see the result before they pay. 2. Employers and brands. Graduate recruiters and student brands already pay societies and careers events to reach students. A sponsored call ("Will 80 people come to the careers evening?") fills their event and tells them who turned up. 3. Students' unions and colleges. They already spend on getting students involved. A licence gives them their own leagues and a view of which events students are actually going to turn up to. 4. Ads in the Rewards section. Any advertiser can appear beside the prizes, through an ad network like Google's or sold directly. It is a placement, not targeting: no personal data is sold. This is small until there are a lot of players. THE ARITHMETIC FOR ONE CAMPUS (Cambridge, 2,250 players: one student in ten) - Venues: 20 venues x 5 challenges a year x £100 = £10,000. That is about three sponsored challenges a week in term time. - Employers and brands: 18 campaigns x £500 = £9,000. - Licence: £10,000. - Ads: each player sees about 6 ad views a week over a 30-week year, which is 405,000 views a campus. At about £3 per 1,000 views (roughly what UK in-app native ads earn through an ad network) that is about £1,200. Sold directly to student brands at £10 per 1,000 it would be about £4,000. - Total about £30,000 a year. Running a campus should cost about £10,000 (student ambassadors on commission, hosting, moderation), which leaves about £20,000. ADS AT SCALE: with 286,000 players, ads bring in roughly £150,000 a year at ad-network rates, or about £500,000 if sold directly. So ads matter nationally, not per campus. IF ASKED "won't ads be most of your revenue?": they already are. Venue challenges, sponsored calls and ads in Rewards are all advertising, and together they are two-thirds of a campus's revenue. We sell most of it as challenges and not banners because it pays far more: £100 for a challenge that about 2,000 players see is roughly £50 per 1,000 views, against about £3 from an ad network like Google's. For comparison, Snapchat, which people open many times a day, makes about £11 a year from each daily user in Europe. HOW IT SHIFTS: year 1 is venues only. Once national, sponsored calls and ads from employers and brands become the largest share, because they buy every campus in one deal while venues are signed one at a time. HOW WE WILL PROVE IT: free first challenges with a few venues this term, then paid ones. The six-month goal is ten venues that have paid for a challenge. If venues will not pay, we find out in weeks, for almost nothing. IF ASKED "what if venues don't pay?": then employers and unions carry it; a campus still works at about £19,000 a year without venues, because it costs about £10,000 to run. The £10,000 split maps to your three headings: software expertise (£5,500), maintenance (£2,000), referral incentives (£2,500). Every price here is a target, not a result.

Back-up · the rules

How scoring and the crowd's odds work

Your confidenceIf rightIf wrong
Hunch+100
Fairly sure+15−10
Certain+20−30

The points are set so that honesty pays. On average, Hunch scores best if you are up to about 67% sure, Fairly sure between 67% and 80%, and Certain only above 80%.

Points cannot be bought and have no cash value, so nobody can lose anything they own.

Weighted by confidence

The crowd's odds average every call as a probability, so a Certain call moves it more than a Hunch.

Steady from the first call

Every question starts at 50%, so a handful of early calls cannot swing it to an extreme.

Independent answers

The odds stay hidden until you have made your own call, so nobody copies the crowd.

Scored on the server

Calls lock once made and when a question closes. Nobody can edit their own score.

For "how do the points work?" and "is the crowd number just a poll?". The key line: the scoring is designed so that saying how sure you really are is always the best strategy, which is what makes the crowd's odds meaningful.

Where £1.34 comes from

Target revenue of £30,200 a year at Cambridge, divided by its 22,565 students. It assumes one student in ten plays. A planning figure, not a result.

Beyond campus

Local businesses in the US will spend $186.1bn on local advertising in 2026. Total UK advertising was £46.7bn in 2025.

Comparables

BeReal began on campuses and sold for €500m in 2024, with over 40 million users. Strava, a social network built on real-life activity, was valued at $2.2bn in 2025. Valuations, not our market.

Sources: HESA · NCES · UNESCO · BIA Advisory · Advertising Association / WARC · TechCrunch · Strava

For "how big is this, really?". Be straightforward: campus alone is a business of hundreds of millions at global scale, not billions. The reason to back it is that campus is the densest, cheapest place to prove a product that then works for any community with a calendar, and that market is local advertising.

Why the big platforms cannot simply add this: feeds and group chats do not know a community's calendar, fantasy games only cover national sport, and anonymous apps cannot earn a university's endorsement.

Back-up · trust and regulation

A game, not a bet: the detail

No money, by design

Nothing to buy, stake or cash out. In Great Britain, free draws and prize competitions with no payment to enter sit outside the Gambling Act 2005. We will take legal advice before scaling.

A real community

Institutional email addresses only, and first names on show. Verified login replaces the pilot's simple join before any wider launch.

Rules against harm

No calls about relationships, health, appearance or grades. A call about a named person will need that person's consent, and they can remove it.

Moderated, and yours to leave

Organisers post the official calls and review every suggestion. Comments can be removed. Anyone can delete their account and data in one tap.

Source: Gambling Commission guidance on prize competitions and free draws

For "isn't this gambling?" and "what stops it turning nasty?". Short answer to the first: no money goes in, so there is nothing to lose; it is a free prize competition. Short answer to the second: the rules are built in, not bolted on: banned topics are blocked by the app, organisers approve every question, and named people must consent.

Back-up · risks

What could go wrong, and our answer

RiskOur answer
A new community starts emptyOrganisers post official calls from day one, so the feed is never empty.
The novelty fadesWeekly reveals, seasons that reset, real prizes and friends' groups.
A call embarrasses someoneBanned topics are blocked, named people must consent, organisers moderate.
It is seen as gamblingNo money anywhere. Built for a university to endorse; legal advice before scaling.
Partners do not payPrice and pay-per-visit are tested with pilot partners before we expand.
A big platform copies itTheir unit is the feed. Ours is the community, and its trust.
For "what keeps you up at night?". Pick one honestly: retention. Lots of social apps get a great first week. The pilot's first measure is whether people who joined in week one are still making calls in week four.
